title: Microscopic Dynamical Entropy II: Statistical and Stochastic Thermodynamics of Hamiltonian Systems
abstract: The Microscopic Dynamical Entropy (MDE) introduced in Ref. [1] describes irreversible relaxation of selected variables x within a finite closed Hamiltonian system of fixed total energy E. Here we extend the framework to arbitrary total-energy distributions and time-dependent Hamiltonians. This allows work interactions with external agents or protocols, crucial in stochastic and classical thermodynamics, and driven systems more generally, to be addressed directly. The central step is to reduce the full microscopic description in terms of selected variables x and unmonitored variables y to one in terms of the selected variables and the instantaneous total energy (x,E). The unmonitored degrees of freedom y in Y enter through their conditional phase-space volume (CPV) $Ω_Y(x,E,t)$. This construction allows work and heat to be defined directly for finite Hamiltonian composites, including cases where Y is so small that its temperature is not well defined. We demonstrate monotonic MDE growth, corresponding to the macroscopic second law, under mixing and time-scale separation even for driven systems with arbitrary energy distributions. At trajectory level, we derive detailed and integral fluctuation relations for the MDE, generalising standard large-bath results. We verify these numerically in a driven few-particle Hamiltonian system, showing the emergence of stochastic thermodynamics for collective coordinates, such as the centre-of-mass position, even in closed systems with only ten or twenty degrees of freedom. Physically, these fluctuation relations connect irreversibility to the change in the number of unmonitored microstates compatible with initial and final data for the observed coordinates. Together, our results provide a finite-system Hamiltonian foundation for the emergence of classical and stochastic thermodynamics and extend their applicability to surprisingly small heat baths.
summary: The paper introduces the Microscopic Dynamical Entropy (MDE) to quantify entropy production in finite, closed Hamiltonian systems. It extends this framework to handle time-dependent driving and variable total energy by reducing the description to observed coordinates ($x$) and instantaneous energy ($E$). The key achievement is deriving fluctuation theorems that connect macroscopic irreversibility directly to geometric properties of the unobserved phase space volume.
main_problem: The paper develops a microscopic framework to derive thermodynamic irreversibility (the second law) for finite, closed Hamiltonian systems by analyzing the entropy associated with coarse-graining the full phase space.
main_result: It successfully derives detailed and integral fluctuation theorems connecting non-equilibrium work/heat exchange to changes in the conditional phase-space volume ($\Omega_Y$), confirming that irreversibility emerges from the choice of observation variables.
method: The core method involves defining the Microscopic Dynamical Entropy (MDE) based on partitioning degrees of freedom into observed ($x$) and unobserved ($y$) parts, allowing for extensions to time-dependent Hamiltonians and variable energy distributions.
model_or_system: The system is a finite closed Hamiltonian system $XY$, where dynamics are governed by $H_{XY}(t)$. The analysis reduces the description from $(x, y)$ to $(x, E)$, treating the unobserved variables $y$ as an effective bath whose volume $\Omega_Y(x, E)$ dictates the entropy contribution.
key_observables: Microscopic Dynamical Entropy (MDE), Conditional Phase-Space Volume ($\Omega_Y$), Fluctuation Ratios ($P_F/P_R$), and Energy Distribution $E$.
important_parameters: The system size (e.g., 10 or 20 degrees of freedom for numerical tests) and the time dependence of external driving forces are key parameters.
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on assuming Hamiltonian reversibility and making a non-destructive coarse-graining from $(x, y)$ to $(x, E)$.
figures_summary: Numerical simulations confirm the detailed fluctuation theorem by showing that the ratio of forward to reverse probabilities matches the theoretical prediction derived from endpoint phase-space volumes.
paper_structure: The paper builds conceptually by first establishing the MDE for fixed energy (Paper I), then extending it to time-dependent Hamiltonians and variable energy distributions, culminating in the derivation and numerical verification of trajectory-level fluctuation theorems.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, microscopic foundation for non-equilibrium thermodynamics directly within Hamiltonian mechanics, bypassing the need for large bath approximations common in standard stochastic treatments.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: Numerical verification of the endpoint-CPV detailed fluctuation theorem for the driven particle gas. The blue sym- bols show the measured value of log[PF (s)/PR(−s)], where s = ∆smd is computed from Eq. (4.10). The orange line shows the theoretical prediction log[PF (s)/PR(−s)] = s. The agreement confirms that the detailed fluctuation theorem is controlled by the endpoint CPVs, while the intermediate in- teraction and driving only affect the trajectory statistics.
